question: first-clients
summary: The evidence points to a narrow, referral-assisted, proof-heavy path rather than volume outbound. B2B buyers still evaluate on reputation, testimonials and case studies, and 69% are frustrated by hidden pricing, while cold email reply rates have collapsed to about 0.45% across 7.5 million 2025 emails. The best-documented founder funnel (a technical founder selling an AI lead-gen service) turned 487 LinkedIn requests into 8 held calls, 4 signed one-month free pilots and 2 paying clients in 30 days, with roughly 10 hours of unpaid setup per pilot. Free pilots appear to work only when they are short, written, success-measured and pre-priced for conversion; unpaid 'test clients' were described by that same founder as expensive customer-discovery. AI adoption among genuinely small firms is still thin (Census: under 20% of firms with four or fewer employees), so the first five clients will likely come from warm/referral introductions and a narrow niche where the owner already feels the pain, not from a broad 'AI agency' pitch.

findings.finding: B2B buyers start research with search engines far more than with referrals, but referrals still shape the shortlist
findings.evidence: Mixology's 2025 B2B Buyer Report (511 B2B buyers, 48% US / 52% UK) asked where buyers typically start research: search engines 40%, peer recommendations 19%, industry events/conferences 15%, LinkedIn 9%, vendor websites 6%. Yet 58% said they use peer recommendations at some point in evaluating a vendor, versus 19% who start there.

findings.finding: Proof beats credentials: reviews, demos and case studies are how buyers actually evaluate a vendor
findings.evidence: In the same 511-buyer survey, buyers evaluating vendors used customer reviews/testimonials (68%), product demonstrations or free trials (65%), peer recommendations (58%) and case studies/success stories (54%). Case studies were the single most influential content type (42%), ahead of pricing/ROI calculators (18%) and webinars/video demos (18%). When asked what makes a vendor credible: reputation 45%, high-quality content 21%, positive testimonials 21%, certifications or industry awards just 3%.

findings.finding: Hidden pricing is the number-one buyer frustration, which argues for publishing pilot and care-fee prices
findings.evidence: Top frustrations with vendors (511 buyers): lack of clear pricing 69%, aggressive or overly persistent follow-ups 63%, slow response to inquiries 61%, poor understanding of my business needs 56%, generic/irrelevant communication 51%. Preferred first engagement: speak to a sales rep 30%, request a demo or trial 30%, evaluate the website independently 20%. Among respondents at firms under 100 employees, 31% preferred a sales rep, 29% a demo/trial and 25% the website.

findings.finding: Referrals are how professional-services buyers find firms, and firms rarely ask for them
findings.evidence: Hinge Research Institute study of 822 buyers and 533 providers of professional services: the most common way buyers find a new firm is by asking another person (71% of the time); the next most common is online search (11%). Cost tipped the final selection only 8% of the time; reputation was the single most important characteristic. 69% of buyers said they were very willing to recommend their provider, but 'almost three quarters of the time' nobody had asked them.

findings.finding: Even a referred buyer checks you out online first, so a credible site and visible proof are prerequisites
findings.evidence: Hinge's 'Beyond Referrals' study of 1,028 professional-services buyers: over 99% check a firm out before engaging, and the average buyer uses more than three separate strategies. Over 80% visit the firm's website; buyers were 'slightly more likely' to search online about you than to ask a friend or colleague; contacting supplied references was the least-used method, and social media was used more often than contacting references.

findings.finding: Cold email response rates have collapsed, so volume outbound is a weak first-client channel in 2025-26
findings.evidence: Belkins reports a 2025 cross-channel benchmark dataset of 16.5 million cold emails, 20+ million LinkedIn outreach attempts and 5+ million cold calls. Its separate analysis of more than 7.5 million cold emails sent during 2025 (replies counted against all emails to net-new contacts) found an average reply rate of 0.45%: 0.50% in H1 2025, 0.40% in H2 (a 20% decline within the year), and 0.35% in December.

findings.finding: A documented LinkedIn outbound funnel produced 2 paying clients from 487 connection requests in 30 days
findings.evidence: Technical founder Fabian Dietrich (IbexAI, an agency/SaaS hybrid) published 30 days of his main acquisition channel: 487 connection requests sent, 175 accepted (36%), 43 replies (25% of accepted), 15 interested (35% of replies), 11 discovery calls booked, 8 calls held (2 cancelled, 1 no-show), 5 second calls, 4 signed agreements, 4 clients onboarded, 2 pilots finished (2 stopped early), 2 paid clients.

findings.finding: Free pilots worked as a written gating step, but cost roughly 10 hours of setup each and half converted
findings.evidence: Same founder: the pilot was a '1-month free pilot' under a 'very non-committal and friendly-worded 2-page agreement', used to filter out non-serious prospects because each pilot costs '10+ hours of manual setup, scraping costs, and AI credits'. Of 4 pilots, 2 finished and both became paid clients; he adds that 'every client that we have managed to drive results for ended up signing up for the paid plan.' Earlier he said the team 'took on many unpaid test clients to find out who's actually a good customer' and calls high-touch acquisition 'an expensive way to acquire clients'.

findings.finding: Cold outreach to people who publicly described the problem converted far better than generic outreach
findings.evidence: Skyvern's founders listed about 100 people who had posted online asking for LLM-driven browser automation and emailed each one: '~30 people replied'. After calls, 4 agreed to work with them before any product existed, and the first version shipped over a weekend.

findings.finding: High-volume cold email is still reported to work in AI automation, but only in a promotional, self-reported case
findings.evidence: An AI-automation founder interviewed by Millionaire Copy says he sent about 1,000 emails a day, needed about three weeks to get the system working, landed his first client about two weeks later and a second a week after that; he reports 11 clients in January and roughly $19,000 earned in three months, later cutting to about 3,000 emails a week while delivering. The interview is tied to a paid AI course ('AI campus'), so treat the numbers as marketing-adjacent.

findings.finding: Very small firms are still mostly non-users of AI, so the addressable early market is firms with staff, not solo owners
findings.evidence: Census BTOS data for December 14, 2025 to May 3, 2026: overall AI use hovered between 17% and 20% (19.8% as of May 3, 2026); 37% of firms with 250+ employees used AI, 32% of firms with 100-249; use 'didn't change significantly among firms with fewer than 20 employees' and 'less than 20% of firms with four or fewer employees reported using AI'. By sector: Information 39.7%, Finance and Insurance 33.9%, Retail Trade about 14%.

findings.finding: Vendor surveys show much higher 'AI use' because they count any AI-enabled software, a trap when sizing demand
findings.evidence: Thryv's second annual survey (540 US small-business decision-makers, 1-100 employees, $100k-$9.9M revenue, collected May 4-14, 2025) found 55% 'currently using artificial intelligence... including software you have been using that now uses AI', up from 39% in 2024. By size: 68% of 10-100 employee firms, 53% of 5-9, 37% of 1-4. By industry: professional services 71%, restaurant/retail 61%, construction 48%. 80% said AI is necessary to reach new customers and 63% use AI daily, averaging 2.3 business areas.

findings.finding: Practitioners say generalist consulting is saturated and vertical niching is what opens doors
findings.evidence: In a Hacker News thread on landing first consulting projects (item 47822940, thread page itself undated), a startup CEO wrote that general consultancy is 'an extremely crowded space' and that he receives at least three emails a week from software agencies and consultants, advising would-be consultants to become an expert in one thing, show a face and location, and network. Another commenter who had done generalist consulting for six years said he had pivoted to executive-search firms and was 'already starting to see the fruits': 'Many potential customers seem happy to open the door and chat.'

findings.finding: A paid pilot needs a price, a decision-maker, a success measure and an end date; free pilots only when learning is capped and explicit
findings.evidence: Purdue's buildpurdue program guidance: 'A paid pilot does not need to be expensive. It needs a price, a decision-maker, a success measure, and an end date. If you cannot name those four things, keep the engagement as discovery or decline it.' It permits a free pilot only when 'you are deliberately buying learning and the cost is capped', with defined workflow access, structured feedback and a scheduled decision at the end, and warns that a customer expecting production support or custom features is 'a paid engagement with an uncomfortable price conversation delayed'.

resources.name: Mixology Digital, The B2B Buyer Report 2025
resources.what_it_offers: Free 55-page survey report of 511 B2B buyers (US/UK) covering where buyers start research, how they evaluate vendors, what content influences them, preferred first engagement and top frustrations, broken out by company size.
resources.how_to_use_it: Use the company-size breakouts to justify a one-page website with published pilot pricing, two or three proof items (case study/demo/review) and a 'book a 20-minute call' path; benchmark our own close rate against its evaluation-stage numbers.

resources.name: Hinge Research Institute buyer studies (Inside the Buyer's Brain / Beyond Referrals)
resources.what_it_offers: Free executive summaries and reports on how professional-services buyers find, check out and select firms, with sample sizes stated (822 buyers/533 providers; 1,028 buyers; 1,914 buyers/3,160 sellers for the 4th edition).
resources.cost: Free (executive summary and selected reports); industry reports sometimes paid/pre-order
resources.how_to_use_it: Model the referral-plus-verification path: build the referral ask into every pilot close, and make the website answer what a referred buyer checks (who you are, niche, proof, pricing).

resources.name: Submit.co 'How 233 startups got their first users' case database
resources.what_it_offers: Filterable library of first-customer stories with reported funnel numbers and a link to each primary post (e.g. 487 LinkedIn requests to 2 paid clients; ~100 cold emails to 4 design partners).
resources.how_to_use_it: Pull the B2B/agency and cold-outreach entries to set realistic funnel assumptions and to find first-hand write-ups worth reading in full before choosing channels.

resources.name: The Next Web / Belkins cold outreach benchmark analysis
resources.what_it_offers: Free article reporting 2025 reply-rate benchmarks across 7.5 million cold emails (0.45% average) plus a larger cross-channel dataset (16.5M emails, 20M+ LinkedIn attempts, 5M+ calls), with a methodology caveat about changing denominators.
resources.how_to_use_it: Use it to set expectations for any cold-email test: a few hundred sends should be expected to yield single-digit replies, so pair email with LinkedIn/community and do not judge a channel on one week.

resources.name: NJSBDC at Rutgers University-New Brunswick (serves Middlesex County)
resources.what_it_offers: One-on-one small-business counseling and training, currently delivered virtually; NJSBDC states 'nearly all of our services are provided at no cost'. Counselors cover business plans, marketing, sales, financials and certifications.
resources.cost: No cost ('nearly all of our services are provided at no cost')
resources.how_to_use_it: Register through the eRFC/consulting request form (required before any service) and use a counselor as a free second opinion on pricing, the pilot contract and side-business structure; ask whether they will introduce us to local professional-services owners.

resources.name: BNI Northern New Jersey chapter membership
resources.what_it_offers: Weekly referral-based networking chapters with a seat exclusivity per profession; published fee schedule for new members.
resources.cost: $200 application fee plus $760 for one year = $960 first year; $1,500 for two years; $3,200 for five years (fees non-refundable on acceptance)
resources.how_to_use_it: Visit several chapters as a guest before paying, and only join one where the seat for 'AI automation / IT consultant' is free and the members already serve our target niches (law, insurance, property management).

resources.name: U.S. Census Bureau Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS), AI supplement
resources.what_it_offers: Free, biweekly, nationally representative firm-level data on AI use and expected use, including breakouts by firm size and sector, plus a 15-business-function AI supplement collected since November 17, 2025.
resources.how_to_use_it: Cite size/sector adoption rates in our pitch and use the supplement's reasons-for-not-using data to design the first conversation (education/diagnostic) for 5-200 employee firms.

resources.name: Thryv AI and Small Business Adoption 2025 survey
resources.what_it_offers: Free 22-page vendor survey of 540 US small businesses (1-100 employees) with methodology, adoption by employee count and industry, top use areas and time/money-saved claims.
resources.how_to_use_it: Mine the industry breakouts (professional services 71%, restaurant/retail 61%, construction 48%) and use-case rankings to pick the first niche and the first agent to productize; treat the headline adoption number as vendor-framed, not a market size.

resources.name: buildpurdue pilot-pricing guidance
resources.what_it_offers: Free written framework and checklist for scoping and charging for a startup pilot, including the five questions a pilot agreement should answer and when a free pilot is defensible.
resources.cost: Free (article); separate cohort program referenced on the page
resources.how_to_use_it: Turn it into our one-page pilot agreement template: owner with authority, one workflow, deliverables, success measure, end-date decision and the pre-agreed monthly care fee if it converts.

recommendations_for_us: Inference: run two channels only for the first 90 days - warm/referral introductions (including referral partners such as bookkeepers, MSPs and insurance brokers who already serve our niches) and targeted LinkedIn/email to owners who publicly describe the pain. Hinge's 71% referral finding and the 0.45% cold-email reply benchmark together say broad outbound will burn a side-business founder's limited evenings.

Inference: budget the funnel from the one documented case rather than optimism - roughly 100 targeted LinkedIn touches per held call, ~2 held calls per signed pilot, and about 1 paying client per 2 pilots. For 3 clients, plan ~300-500 targeted touches and 6+ pilots over 2-3 months; do not quit the day job on a 30-day sample.

Inference: sell a fixed-price paid pilot (for example a 4-week after-hours intake agent at a low four-figure fee, credited toward set-up) and publish the price and the monthly care fee on the site. 69% of buyers call hidden pricing their top frustration, and paid commitment is a cleaner demand test than a free build.

Inference: if we give a pilot away, make it a written 30-day pilot with a named owner, one measurable outcome (calls answered, response time, documents processed), a scheduled conversion decision and the care fee agreed up front - the model that produced 2 paid clients from 4 pilots, at a stated cost of ~10 hours of setup each. Cap it at one or two at a time given the day job.

Inference: manufacture proof instead of waiting for clients. Record two short demos per target niche using sample data, publish a one-page teardown of a typical firm's intake flow, and label them 'demonstration, not a client result'. Buyers evaluate on demos (65%) and case studies (54%), and over 80% visit the website before engaging.

Inference: pick one niche for the first three clients - professional services or insurance look strongest (Thryv: 71% of professional services; Census: 33.9% of finance/insurance use AI) - and build one repeatable offer, one demo and one referral ask per niche. Generalist positioning is what practitioners describe as crowded and price-compressed.

Inference: answer inbound within hours and follow up at most a few times with something useful. Slow response (61%) and aggressive follow-up (63%) are among buyers' top frustrations, and a referred buyer who is chased too hard never reaches out.

Inference: make the referral ask an explicit step in every pilot close (a short script plus a one-page summary the client can forward), because Hinge found buyers willing to refer but firms almost never asking.

Inference: before paying for any networking membership ($960 first year at BNI Northern NJ, non-refundable), guest-visit 4-6 chapters and check that our buyer is in the room; treat it as a 6-12 month referral investment, not a first-client channel.

pitfalls.pitfall: Treating cold email volume as a strategy: reply rates averaged 0.45% across 7.5M emails in 2025 and fell through the year, and sender reputation is easily damaged (Google's guidance is a spam-complaint rate under 0.1%).
Open-ended free pilots: a pilot without a price, decision-maker, success measure and end date becomes unpaid consulting and product management for one account.
Underestimating pilot delivery cost: the documented AI pilot consumed 10+ hours of manual setup plus scraping and AI-credit costs, and 2 of 4 pilots stopped early.
Buying credibility signals that buyers ignore: certifications and industry awards influenced only 3% of buyers, while reputation (45%) and testimonials (21%) dominated.

Using vendor-survey AI adoption (55% of SMBs) as the market size when Census BTOS shows 17-20% overall and under 20% for the smallest firms - it leads to overestimating how warm the average small firm is.
Paying non-refundable networking dues before testing the room: BNI Northern NJ charges $960 for the first year and states fees are non-refundable on acceptance.

caveats: Mixology's 511-buyer sample skews to larger organisations (39% under 100 employees; 23% over $100M revenue) and is half UK, so percentages are directional for 5-200 employee Middlesex County firms, not predictive.

Both Hinge studies are older (article pages undated; one references a 2009 baseline) but are the closest professional-services-specific buyer data found; treat the percentages as historical benchmarks.

Founder-reported funnels (Fabian Dietrich, Skyvern, 'Igor') are single, self-published accounts; only Dietrich's reports a full funnel over a 30-day window with denominators, and the Igor interview is tied to a paid course.
Thryv is a vendor selling SMB software and defines AI use to include software that 'now uses AI', which explains much of the gap with Census BTOS.

Census BTOS measures AI use in the past two weeks and changed its question wording in November 2025 (from producing goods/services to any business function), so pre- and post-change rates are not strictly comparable.
No source found measures close rates or payback specifically for AI-agent consultancies selling to 5-200 employee US firms; all funnel benchmarks here are borrowed from adjacent B2B services or SaaS.
The referral-heavy picture comes from professional-services buyers generally; no NJ-specific buying survey was located.
data_gaps: Reddit threads (r/AiAutomations '6 weeks in, no clients', r/EmailOutreach '1,104 emails, 0 paying', r/AI_Agents 2025 year-in-review) could not be fetched (JavaScript/blocked), so those anecdotes are excluded rather than cited from snippets.
Clutch's B2B buying report (451 respondents, referrals 55%/53%) and the Agency Management Institute AgencyEdge 2024 PDF both returned HTTP 403 and were not used.
SCORE New Jersey pages (free mentoring) returned HTTP 403, so SCORE could not be verified as a resource despite being a likely fit.
ABA and Clio 2025 law-firm AI adoption figures (roughly 20% of firms under 50 lawyers; 8% of solos for Clio) appeared only in search summaries - the source pages returned 403, so they are excluded.
Census County Business Patterns API requires a key, so a count of law firms, insurance agencies, property managers and contractors in Middlesex County could not be produced to size the niches.
No public survey or dataset was found on what AI-automation agencies actually charge for pilots or on their pilot-to-paid conversion rates beyond individual founder posts.
